World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Fire service 'not fit for purpose' in regional SA, uncovered report finds
World.content:
South Australia's regional Metropolitan Fire Service is "underfunded", "under-resourced", and "not fit for purpose" in many instances, a previously secret report has found.

The review raised concerns about all 17 regional MFS stations, singling out Port Pirie, home to a major smelter, and Mount Gambier, the state's timber processing hub.

Through Freedom of Information, the ABC obtained the report, "A review of the SA MFS regional operations", by former Tasmania Fire Service chief Dermot Barry, handed down in September 2024.

It was commissioned by the MFS, at the request of the United Firefighters' Union (UFU), which told the ABC that regional communities were at risk of a "catastrophic event" due to the problems.

Mr Barry determined "[were] it not for the desire of the regional staff to make their communities safe … regional operations would be completely dysfunctional", largely owing to training shortfalls and "low morale".

An MFS spokesperson said it "considered all recommendations, with more than half implemented or progressed", but the UFU says many of the identified issues persist.

'Difficult to justify' level of training

Mr Barry wrote that Regional Operations was "underfunded and under-resourced for its purpose and unsustainable in its current state."

"Many of the facilities and much of their equipment and training is not fit for purpose and poses a significant risk to both the firefighters and the MFS," he said.

Mr Barry's report found that almost 80 per cent of the surveyed retained firefighters believe they are insufficiently trained.

A survey included in the report found over 80 per cent of regional firefighters surveyed "believed that their stations, trucks and equipment are not fit for purpose", while almost 80 per cent of retained firefighter respondents "believe they are 'insufficiently trained'".

Part-time retained staff solely man 15 regional MFS stations, with full-time staff known as career firefighters also employed at Mount Gambier and Port Pirie.

Retained firefighters receive six days of initial training before deployment, compared to 16 weeks for career recruits, the report said.

Mr Barry said "it would seem inevitable that this level of training and support will be tested in a court … and there is a very real risk of an adverse finding".

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with George Yankovich at george.yankovich@proton.me

However, when firefighters request training in Adelaide, "they believe their application is … 'tainted' by the requirement for the MFS to pay them travelling allowances".

"This almost always results in rejection," Mr Barry said.

An MFS spokesperson said a "review of training programs" would commence this year, at the UFU's request.

"All recruit firefighters must complete mandatory training, including breathing apparatus and structural firefighting, before commencing operational duties, with expanded training conditions and remuneration," they said.

Heavy rescue equipment being used in a road crash rescue. (Supplied: Tasmania Fire Service)

Fleet gaps a problem

Mount Gambier councillor Paul Jenner — speaking on his own behalf — said he "wasn't surprised" by the report, having lobbied for new MFS appliances since the mid-2000s.

However, he was concerned by recent gaps left in the local service's fleet.

Paul Jenner has been lobbying for new MFS appliances since the mid-2000s. (ABC News: Joshua Brine)

For example, the station's Combined Aerial Pump Appliance (CAPA) — designed for high-altitude structure fires — was away for servicing during the fire season.

Mount Gambier has several timber mills which require the appliance, according to Mr Jenner.

"It was only meant to be there for a few months and it was gone for nine months at least," he said.

" If something happened [at a mill], a vehicle would have to come from Warrnambool which would take two and a half hours … there wouldn't be much of it left. "

A CAPA appliance in action at a fire in Stirling, in the Adelaide Hills. (Supplied: CFS)

'Not-insignificant funding' needed, union says

UFU secretary Peter Russell said the union asked the MFS to commission a review following members' complaints.

He believed the MFS "wants to improve conditions" but needs a "not-insignificant funding injection … to provide a safe level of service".

"Regional resourcing has been a problem for a very long time and it's led to significant member dissatisfaction," he said.

Peter Russell says the review was initiated by the MFS on the back of complaints from serving personnel. (ABC News: Luke Pike)

"I've had reports from retained stations saying there are reasonably long-serving retained members that have never had proper structural firefighting training," he said, referring to live drills.

" There are periods up to five years where they haven't had road crash rescue training [refreshers]. There is constant stopping and starting for HAZMAT training, where they begin, never finish it, the course changes, and they start again. "

The Productivity Commission found that funding per head of population for SA firefighters is $154 — the lowest in the country compared to the national average of $250.

"Although we have the best firefighters, they're not being given the best opportunities for training, because we're told the MFS can simply not afford it," he said.

"That eventually has to present a community risk … it's a reality that if the government doesn't reconsider the funding, there will eventually be a catastrophic event that could have been prevented."

Government quiet on review, but 'ensuring support'

In a statement, Emergency Services Minister Rhiannon Pearce did not comment directly on the review, but said the "government is ensuring [firefighters] have the support, recognition and compensation for this crucial, often dangerous work".

This included a pay rise, new appliances, and expanding cancer compensation.

Emergency Services Minister Rhiannon Pearce. (ABC News)

The MFS spokesperson also said: "Upgraded and modern rescue appliances are replacing decades-old vehicles, strengthening emergency response capability across regional areas, with further rollouts planned in coming months."

They said retained firefighters have been offered "increased remuneration and retainer allowances, enhanced training support, and an expanded incident response time to broaden recruitment opportunities".

World.title: Bondi royal commission to hear challenge to antisemitism definition
World.content:
A royal commission sparked by the Bondi terror attack is this week expected to hear from groups who challenge the commission's accepted definition of antisemitism, as well as expert witnesses from the United Kingdom.

Dozens of people from the Jewish community last week gave evidence to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, with some sessions closed to the public for security reasons.

Hearings will continue this week, with some sessions to start earlier to accommodate the witnesses in overseas time zones.

Royal Commissioner Virginia Bell flagged the inquiry had received a number of submissions from some Jewish people and others who believed the definition of antisemitism the inquiry adopted could be "weaponised in order to suppress criticism of Israel".

Former High Court Justice Virginia Bell is heading the royal commission. (Supplied: Murray Harris Photography)

The inquiry has accepted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, which describes a "certain perception of Jews which may be expressed as a hatred towards Jews."

"Rhetorical and physical manifestations of antisemitism are directed toward Jewish or non-Jewish individuals and/or their property, toward Jewish community institutions and religious facilities," the definition states.

Commissioner Bell has granted limited leave to the Jewish Council of Australia, who are expected to appear this week, to ask questions of the expert witnesses giving evidence about the IHRA definition.

The commission will continue to hear from people with lived experience of antisemitism, with previous witnesses providing examples from within schools, workplaces, sporting organisations and universities.

Some witnesses have been given pseudonyms after expressing concern about potential backlash related to their appearance at the commission.

The royal commission hears from a number of anonymous witnesses due to safety concerns. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The hearings have been heavily policed, with officers moving on and later charging a man who allegedly wore a swastika shirt outside the building.

More hearing dates announced

A second block of hearings has been announced for May 25, with the sessions to focus on the circumstances surrounding the Bondi terror attack.

It is expected to examine:

The terrorism threat level and security environment in the lead-up to the attack;

The conduct of security, intelligence and law enforcement agencies relevant to the attack, including what was known about the shooters and what was done with that information;

The security arrangements for the Chanukah by the Sea event;

How intelligence is utilised and shared to inform decisions made by security, intelligence and law enforcement agencies;

Resourcing for counter-terrorism, and the effectiveness of current powers, systems and processes of security, intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

The commission has received more than 9,600 submissions, with the majority identifying as Jewish.

Antisemitism royal commission delivers first report The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has released its interim report, making 14 recommendations.

Most are located in New South Wales and Victoria, and a large number of submissions give examples of lived experience with antisemitism.

Commissioner Bell said many who have made submissions have been interviewed by the inquiry's solicitors.

"We have assembled a team of analysts who review every submission that we receive, and each submission is referred by subject matter to our legal teams," she said last week.

"I thank all the members of the Jewish community who have already told their stories to the commission and I encourage those who have not yet made a submission to do so."

Submissions will remain open until June 14.

World.title: 'Nuisance' showers for much of Queensland and 'unseasonable' rain in the west
World.content:
Showers and blustery winds are set to greet much of Queensland this week, temporarily abandoning the recent cool autumn mornings.

Parts of the state recorded their coldest mornings so far this year last Friday, with temperatures dipping below freezing on the Granite Belt, but the cool change won't stick around for long, with unsettled conditions ahead.

Senior forecaster from the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) Felim Hanniffy said frequent, nuisance showers were to be expected for much of eastern Queensland from today.

"It's not huge totals, but there will be daily frequent showers with localised moderate falls possible," he said.

"Particularly for the north tropical coast, even exposed coastal areas like the Wide Bay and Sunshine Coast."

'Unseasonable' rain likely for north-west

But the rain wasn't expected to filter from the east coast to the area most in need, the southern Darling Downs.

Further inland, a cloud band developing near Mount Isa could deliver unseasonable rain for the region on Monday, Mr Hanniffy said.

Falls between 10 and 20 millimetres are likely, more than double the monthly average for May in parts of western Queensland.

"We'll see the focus of that activity contract further south across into the Channel Country through the week, certainly around Birdsville," he said.

"Further falls could be multiple times that region's monthly average."

Overnight minimums are expected to peak between 2 and 5 degrees above average, bringing warmer sleeping conditions for much of the state.

Strong wind warning offshore

A strong wind warning is in place across the north and tropical Queensland coast.

Mr Hanniffy said a dominant high pressure system in the Great Australian Bight was moving east, pushing onshore wind and showers along the east coast.

"There are wind warnings for much of the far north, those will become more extensive about the east coast as we head through the week," the forecaster said.

Mr Hanniffy said the combination of weather systems could deliver big swell, but it wasn't likely to reach the warning level.

"There's a risk the offshore southerly swell could filter in closer to the coast Monday, and bring deceptively powerful swells along the south-east coast," he said.

World.title: 'Incredibly concerned': Zero dog fighting-related charges laid in years
World.content:
The number of charges addressing illegal dog fighting in Queensland has plummeted to zero in the years since a special taskforce was disbanded, the ABC can reveal.

The dog fighting and cockfighting unit was formed in 2017 and sat within RSPCA Queensland, staffed by three officers.

Under the unit, the RSPCA achieved its first "major breakthrough" in a decade, with a dog fighting raid that resulted in the seizure of 56 dogs in 2018.

In the 2020-21 financial year, 15 defendants faced 63 charges relating to a prohibited event under the Animal Care and Protection Act. (Supplied)

RSPCA Queensland told the ABC last year, "Australians may be shocked to learn the extent of (dog fighting) operations."

But the work of the specialist unit concluded in mid-2021 and data obtained by the ABC shows that from July 1, 2022 until April 13, 2026 , there were no charges associated with a 'prohibited event' (dog fighting and cockfighting), under the Animal Care and Protection Act.

Dramatic drop in cases prosecuted by RSPCA A man has been charged with animal cruelty a year after neighbours first made a complaint to the RSPCA.

By comparison, dozens of charges were filed in the two financial years prior. Fifteen defendants faced 63 charges relating to a prohibited event under the Act in the 2020-21 financial year, and in 2021-22, there were six charges against two defendants, according to the data from Queensland's Department of Justice.

An ABC investigation last year uncovered international links between the underground world of dog fighting and Australia.

It also revealed that one man, who was jailed for his role in a dog fighting ring, remained a member of multiple online groups that discussed the blood sport and had boasted that he had killed "more dogs than parvovirus".

From July 1 2022 until April 13 2026 there were no charges associated with a 'prohibited event' (dog fighting and cockfighting), under the Animal Care and Protection Act. (Supplied)

Alicia Bennett, a PhD candidate with the Griffith Law School and a former QPS Detective Sergeant, said she was "incredibly concerned" about the lack of charges, saying it was "naïve to assume animal fighting does not continue to exist in Queensland".

"I have spoken to many current and former RSPCA inspectors who believe that dog and cock fighting continue undetected in Queensland," she said.

Dr Steven White, a lecturer in animal law at Griffith University, was also worried about the statistics.

Steven White, Griffith University specialist in animal welfare law. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

"This is clearly a concern, given these activities are likely to still be occurring. Or, at least, if there is no active monitoring of this area, we can't know whether they are decreasing in number [or] increasing," he said.

'Dysfunctional' system

Changes to the administration of the Animal Care and Protection Act (ACPA) in 2022 meant the RSCPA and Queensland Police could no longer prosecute offences, such as dog fighting, without the permission of the Department of Primary Industries.

An "unintended consequence" of this change was cleared up in February by the Queensland government, so that QPS could independently prosecute under the Act again.

Ms Bennett said the fact that the error was not rectified in three years "demonstrates that the system is dysfunctional and co-regulatory authorities are not collaborating effectively".

Outside of the ACPA, Ms Bennett said there were only two offences that police could apply to prohibited events — serious animal cruelty and injuring animals -- but they would be unlikely to capture dog fighting.

"If police arrived at a general dog fighting property where there were several dogs tethered to heavy chains, with scarring associated with dog fighting (but no current serious injury), police would not be able to apply either of the Codes of Offences," she said.

"They might be able to if there was video of the accused perpetrating the cruelty or injury, but that is a long shot," she said.

The RSPCA still needs permission from the department to prosecute offences.

The charity told a 2022 parliamentary committee that it historically took the lead on animal fighting investigations, assisted by QPS.

An RSPCA employee says law changes have made seeking justice for animal abuse a 'convoluted process.' (ABC News: Nickoles Coleman)

But two former RSPCA inspectors told the ABC that in 2022 they were told by the department not to investigate dog fighting and to refer matters to police.

"RSPCA had the muzzle put on," one of the former inspectors said.

In a statement, RSPCA Queensland said "we now use an integrated, multi-agency model that combines our animal welfare expertise with Queensland Police Service leadership on the criminal aspects of these matters".

In 2021, the same year the unit concluded, there were media reports that a man was sacked from RSPCA Queensland after having a sexual relationship with a woman who was under investigation for alleged involvement in dog fighting.

But one inspector said the allegations related to one individual. They argued that a wealth of specialist knowledge about dog fighting and cockfighting was lost when the taskforce was broken up.

Two former RSPCA inspectors told the ABC they were told by the Department of Primary Industries to refer dog fighting matters to police. (ABC News: Nickoles Coleman)

The unit had received training from specialist investigators like Janette Reever, who worked with the FBI to take down a major dog fighting pit in the United States across five jurisdictions.

"The Queensland RSPCA were making a dent in the underground world of dog fighting," she said.

"Without the task force, dog fighters are again operating with impunity and their criminal activities continue with no repercussions."

A former inspector said the taskforce "was something the public supported, and we were getting traction".

The former inspector said their colleagues had concerns about investigators being harassed by those accused of dog fighting.

"Inspectors would stop and change uniforms before heading home, they didn't want anyone to know where they lived," they said.

Australia's links to the illegal blood sport of dog fighting Warning: This story contains graphic images and content involving animal cruelty.

Ms Bennett said dog fighting is a covert activity, and police "lack the expertise to identify these complex and clandestine offences".

" (This) means they are falling through the cracks, along with the animals who are injured and killed as a result of these criminal enterprises. "

A QPS spokesperson said the service "takes all reports of criminal animal behaviour seriously and investigates these occurrences on a case-by-case basis".

"The QPS also welcomes recent legislation amendments, which strengthens the ability of our officers to be more proactive in these types of investigations and allows for more appropriate action in certain matters," they said.

Calls for independent regulation

In Queensland, organising and participating in dog fighting carries a maximum penalty of one year's imprisonment or a $50,070 fine.

That is below the maximum penalty for animal cruelty, which is three years' imprisonment or $333,800.

The people behind several of the state's most high-profile dog fighting cases have served less than half of the maximum penalty behind bars.

In the 2020-21 financial year, 15 defendants faced 63 charges relating to a prohibited event under the Animal Care and Protection Act. (Supplied)

The RSPCA has previously argued that dog fighting penalties should be increased and new offences created to capture the possession of dog fighting paraphernalia.

Ms Bennett said QPS officers should also receive training related to animal welfare offences and signs that dog fighting is occurring.

She said she believes there should be a formal Memorandum of Understanding between the QPS and RSPCA for information-sharing, and argued animal welfare should be transitioned to an independent regulatory authority.

"Without a well-resourced, targeted law enforcement, intelligence-led approach, it will remain undetected, and animals will continue to be injured and killed as a result," she said.

In a joint statement, the DPI and RSPCA Queensland said the "DPI administers the Animal Care and Protection Act 2001 (ACPA) and is the Queensland Government's lead agency for matters of animal welfare, including dog fighting and cock fighting."

"If it appears that other serious criminal activity is present … it may be appropriate to transfer the case to the Queensland Police Service."

The spokesperson said, "investigations into animal welfare matters can cause physical and psychological safety risks to inspectors of both DPI and RSCPA, and this is taken very seriously," the spokesperson said.

"Any threats or harassment towards inspectors are not tolerated and would be reported to QPS immediately."

World.title: Icebreaker's costly refuelling detour could take years to fix
World.content:
A costly refuelling issue affecting Australia's Antarctic icebreaker remains unresolved months out from a key deadline, with internal government documents revealing most fixes could take up to three years to implement.

The RSV Nuyina, which has its home port at Macquarie Wharf in Hobart, has been forced to refuel at Burnie in Tasmania's north-west since 2023.

That's because the Harbour Master rejected an application for the vessel to transit under Hobart's Tasman Bridge so that it could reach the city's marine refuelling depot.

The refusal was linked to safety concerns about the ship's "directional stability", after computer simulations indicated it was at risk of colliding with the bridge's pylons.

RSV Nuyina is not able to pass under Hobart's Tasman Bridge because of safety concerns. (ABC News)

The 674-kilometre detour to Burnie has added almost $900,000 to the Nuyina's annual fuel bill.

In 2024, the Tasmanian government agreed to develop a "refuelling solution" as part of a $188 million deal with the federal government to upgrade the aging Macquarie Wharf.

The funding agreement stipulates that the solution must be accepted by the federal government by the end of July this year and be "available for use" by the next Antarctic season in 2026-27.

The deal includes a $2 million "milestone" payment from the federal government if the state government resolves the situation by the deadline.

Work continues to find 'mutually agreeable' solution

Following the signing of the deal, the state government launched an expression of interest process in early 2025, seeking proposals from the private sector, including for a fuel barge or fuel pipeline.

But government correspondence provided to the ABC under Right to Information (RTI) laws has cast doubt on the prospects of a solution being accepted by the July 31 deadline.

"The Department of State Growth has undertaken industry engagement and market sounding, including an Expressions of Interest process, to identify a solution capable of meeting the timeframe for Milestone 3," the department told the Australian Antarctic Division on February 13.

" State Growth established that a majority of the options assessed, and proposals submitted, involve permanent infrastructure requiring 24 to 36 months to deliver. "

Several additional sentences in the one-page letter were blacked out.

The department's RTI officer said they were redacted because the information included "specific solutions being considered for a potential procurement process", and that its release could expose the department to "competitive disadvantage".

Several sentences of the letter were redacted before it was released. (ABC News)

A separate State Growth letter sent on the same day to the federal environment department said the Tasmanian government remained committed to "fulfilling its requirements" under the terms of the Macquarie Wharf funding agreement.

Late last week, the ABC put a range of questions to State Growth about the status of the refuelling solution, including:

Will a permanent refuelling solution be in place by the start of the 2026-27 season?

If a permanent solution is not in place, is a temporary solution under consideration? If so, what is the temporary solution? Will it be ready for the 2026-27 season?

If a permanent solution is not in place by the deadline, is it correct that the federal government will withhold the $2 million milestone payment? Are there any other penalties?

A State Growth spokesperson did not directly answer the questions, but confirmed work to resolve the issue was continuing.

"We continue to work with the Australian government to identify a mutually agreeable refuelling solution for the RSV Nuyina and look forward to making further announcements in due course," they said.

"The Macquarie Wharf 6 upgrade, including the refuelling solution, reinforces Hobart's strategic role as an Antarctic Gateway City and underscores the economic significance of the Antarctic and Southern Ocean sector to Tasmania."

RSV Nuyina docks at Hobart's aging Macquarie Wharf when in its home port. (Supplied: AAD)

The ABC asked the Australian Antarctic Division (AAD) similar questions.

A spokesperson said the AAD was in "regular discussions" with the state government about possible refuelling options in Hobart.

"The Tasmanian government is responsible for the provision of a suitable refuelling solution for Nuyina, under its agreement with the federal government," they said.

" Until a suitable refuelling solution is delivered, the Australian Antarctic Division will continue to use Port of Burnie to refuel Nuyina. "

The Australian Antarctic Division says it's in "regular discussions" with the state government about possible refuelling options in Hobart. (Pete Harmsen: Australian Antarctic Division)

Polar network calls for swift resolution

One option considered in a 2023 report commissioned by the state government was using road tankers to refuel Nuyina.

But the report noted that 64 road tankers would be needed to fill up the vessel, with each tanker taking at least two hours to transfer its fuel to the ship.

Under that scenario, it would take more than five days, working 24 hours a day, to complete the job.

The RSV Nuyina docked at Hobart's Macquarie Point. (Supplied: AAD)

The Antarctic sector in Tasmania contributes more than $200 million to the state's economy each year, according to a government-commissioned report released last year.

The Tasmanian Polar Network (TPN), which has more than 70 members, including private businesses, education institutions and research bodies, called for a swift resolution to the issue.

"The Tasmanian Polar Network looks forward to a solution for the refuelling of the Nuyina as soon as possible," TPN chair Erin McGoldrick said.

Peter Whish-Wilson chaired an inquiry into funding issues at the Australian Antarctic Division. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Greens Senator Peter Whish-Wilson, who previously chaired a federal inquiry into funding issues at the AAD, said it was imperative that a solution be implemented.

"I'm not sure what it is about this state government and boats and wharves, but this sounds like it's descended into a farce," he said.

"They've had nearly three years since the Nuyina was blocked from going underneath the Tasman Bridge to refuel, and discussions were underway more formally for the last 18 months to find a solution.

"I mean, how hard can it be?

"This is an essential piece of infrastructure for the entire Australian Antarctic Division, which underpins Hobart being the Antarctic gateway."

World.title: An 'outside the square' Bledisloe Cup idea can be a win for Aussie rugby
World.content:
The AFL and NRL have worked hard to achieve the status they enjoy as the pre-eminent football leagues on the domestic stage.

Of course, soccer and rugby union have far greater international presence, but their local competitions trail the AFL and NRL by some margin in terms of popularity.

The number of marquee events the AFL and NRL offer helps consolidate their footing, with the annual Anzac Day matches among those prominent on their respective calendars.

The Collingwood vs Essendon (AFL) and St George Illawarra vs Sydney Roosters (NRL) fixtures attract massive crowds and strong TV viewing figures.

Rugby may soon have its best chance to compete in this space, should the proposed Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test between the Wallabies and All Blacks get the green light.

It is not Rugby Australia's (RA) fault such an event has failed to materialise, as it has backed the idea for a few years.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has been the stumbling block, but its official position could change as early as this week.

NZR has recently expressed support for an Anzac Day Test and it is expected to discuss the proposal further at a board meeting on Thursday.

The All Blacks show off the Bledisloe Cup after their victory in Auckland last year. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

Given the rivalry between Australia and New Zealand in rugby, the code is well-placed to stage an annual Test that encapsulates what Anzac Day means to both countries.

It may also provide rugby with a "State of Origin moment", meaning a sporting event that has the potential to establish a national footprint.

The NRL's State of Origin has moved beyond its heartlands of NSW and Queensland by sparking Australia-wide interest.

Last year's series decider, played in Sydney, attracted a national total TV reach of 5.657 million.

The total TV national average audience was 3.904 million viewers.

To steal a quote from former Australian prime minister Paul Keating, "they are a beautiful set of numbers".

Granted, State of Origin's TV figures would likely be out of reach for an Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test.

But rugby needs to be aspirational and such a match is an ideal opportunity to achieve greater national appeal on an annual basis.

As NSW Waratahs coach Dan McKellar said last week: ""Rugby union needs to grow, it needs to think outside the square."

The Wallaroos played the Black Ferns on Anzac Day this year. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

As has been mooted, a Wallaroos vs Black Ferns Test is set to be included alongside the proposed Bledisloe Cup match.

This should be a priority in any plans devised by RA and NZR, should an agreement be finalised.

The two sides met on the evening of Anzac Day this year and enjoyed promising broadcast ratings, finishing 11th on VOZ's April 25 rankings with a total TV national reach of 887,000 viewers.

It is not a stretch to describe the Wallaroos as a sleeping giant among Australia's national representative teams.

Creating a full-time Wallaroos program is on RA's agenda and increasing their exposure will only boost interest in the team ahead of the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.

Reds cop dubious calls

Publicly, the Queensland Reds chose to be tactful when reflecting on referee Marcus Playle's performance in their 31-21 loss to the Chiefs in Brisbane.

But behind closed doors, they had every right to be seething over several of Playle's decisions in Friday night's Super Rugby Pacific match.

The Reds were left disappointed after their loss to the Chiefs. (AAP: Jason O'Brien)

The Reds were denied a try on the stroke of half-time when Playle judged Seru Uru to be held up.

Playle consulted TMO Glenn Newman and the decision was made to stick with the on-field call, seemingly based off the use of one camera angle.

A second camera angle, which was available to the match officials and shown on Stan Sport, suggested Uru may have grounded the ball on or over the line.

It deserved further investigation from Playle and Newman.

Among the 12-5 penalty count that went against the Reds was a call to ping Josh Flook for an incorrect entry to a ruck inside the home side's 22, when the Chiefs were leading 24-21 in the 78th minute.

Flook's indiscretion is not in dispute, but the Reds can feel aggrieved as Playle appeared to have missed Chiefs captain Luke Jacobson illegally going off his feet at the breakdown moments before awarding the penalty to the visitors.

The Chiefs opted to take a scrum and scored the match-sealing try through number eight Wallace Sititi from the ensuing play.

Reds skipper Fraser McReight was clearly dejected after the match but refused to adopt the "we wuz robbed" approach.

"There was so much more we left out on the field that we could have done better and left ourselves in a better position, and we weren't able to do that," McReight told Stan Sport.

McReight was on the money with his assessment.

As well as the Reds played against the second-placed Chiefs, they let themselves down with errors at crucial moments of the match, both in attack and defence.

Their lineout also misfired in the first half, as they lost three on their throw.

The "one percenters" count and the Chiefs did a better job nailing these.

They deserved to claim a sixth straight win, despite some questionable refereeing decisions going against the Reds.

Brumbies find winning formula

The loss to the Chiefs saw the Reds slip back to sixth place on the standings, with the ACT Brumbies moving one spot ahead of their local rival.

The musical chairs scenario followed the Brumbies' 32-15 win over the Western Force in Canberra on Saturday night.

The Brumbies' victory was timely as it halted a three-match losing streak threatening to derail their push for a finals berth.

Skipper Ryan Lonergan was superb at scrum half, especially in the opening 40 minutes when he expertly changed the Brumbies' angles of attack deep inside Force territory.

He also crossed the stripe in the second half and finished with a 17-point haul in a display worthy of Wallabies selection.

Ryan Lonergan was outstanding for the Brumbies. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Another of the Brumbies backs to impress was inside centre David Feliuai.

You will see few better long balls than what Feliuai delivered to Ollie Sapsford to set up the Brumbies winger for a first-half try.

The 10th-placed Force are not giving up on their faint finals hopes, despite being nine points adrift of the top six.

They struggled for rhythm in attack, largely because the Brumbies denied fly half Ben Donaldson space and time with the ball.

One of the Force's strengths is their defensive lineout and they gave the Brumbies a major headache in this department.

The home side lost five throws, an area of concern ahead of their final two matches of the regular season.

Tahs lose again across the ditch

The Waratahs slumped to another defeat in New Zealand, this time going down 31-26 to the Highlanders.

A second-half fightback was admirable after the Waratahs trailed 28-7 at the break in Dunedin on Saturday.

They closed the gap to 28-26 with 90 seconds left on the clock, but a late Cam Millar penalty goal gave the Highlanders their final winning margin.

The Waratahs were again reminded professional rugby is an 80-minute game and they only have themselves to blame for falling so far behind on the scoreboard in the first half.

The Waratahs were chasing the Highlanders throughout the match. (Getty Images: Joe Allison)

Their 30-28 win over the Brumbies in Canberra back in round seven showed what they can produce, but that is now a distant memory.

The Waratahs' season has been riddled with inconsistency and they have lost four of their past five matches.

Still, the Waratahs have a slim chance of qualifying for the finals.

They sit in eighth place on the standings, six points behind the Reds.

World.title: 'Do or die': Flick's journey from jail to artist and First Nations mentor
World.content:
Reaching adulthood is usually a cause for celebration, but Flick Chafer-Smith hit rock bottom a day after her 18th birthday when she was sent to jail.

Swept into a grim cycle of drug addiction and reoffending, she spent the next six years in and out of prison until she found her salvation through art.

"It was do or die basically … I was either going to end up in prison for the rest of my life, dead, or I had to change," she said.

"So art was a massive part of helping me do that. I was able to put on canvas things that I wasn't able to vocalise and express through words."

Ms Chafer-Smith was helped by the Victorian Indigenous arts program, The Torch, which engages with First Nations people in jail, providing them with artistic support and connection to culture, as well as financial income from arts sales.

About 500 artworks, many of them paintings, appear in the Confined 17 exhibition. (Supplied: James Henry)

"From a young age, I struggled a lot with addiction, mental health, family violence problems and when I was inside, I only saw myself as a criminal, a drug addict. After a while being told that continuously, you start to believe it," she said.

"But once I started painting and I had my first few sales, I thought, 'Hang on, I can actually make a positive thing and put it out into the world. I can be known for a different reason.'

Ms Chafer-Smith is among 424 artists featured in Confined 17, an exhibition running at Glen Eira Town Hall and organised by The Torch.

Confined 17 is the 17th annual exhibition showcasing the work of First Nations artists with lived experience of incarceration in Victoria.

The 500 or so artworks, which include paintings, weavings, ceramics and carved emu eggs, address themes of kinship, healing, ancestral stories and life journeys.

One hundred per cent of exhibition sales go directly back to the artists who have already been released, while for those still incarcerated, 70 per cent is withheld to help them integrate back into the community after they complete their jail terms.

Chafer-Smith also convenes an art group for former prisoners like her, called Tiddas, which means sister. (ABC News)

But apart from her success in art, Flick is most proud of her role as a First Peoples mentor with the Torch, regularly returning to women's prisons in Victoria to help guide other inmates on their own art-led journey of redemption.

"It's a full circle moment, being able to support those that are going through what I've been through," Ms Chafer-Smith explained.

"It gives them that inspiration and hope that they might not have had before."

She also convenes a monthly art group for former prisoners.

A piece of art created by a member of the monthly Tiddas group. (ABC News)

"The group is called Tiddas, the word for sister. It's incredible seeing my artists thrive and achieve their goals in life: being able to be independent, never looking back towards jail," Ms Chafer-Smith said.

"Those things really fill my cup."

One of the artists she's mentored, Narnz, credits her friend Flick for turning her life around.

(Left to right) Narnz, Eli, Flick Chafer-Smith and Ashantii at the exhibition. (Supplied)

"It was absolutely amazing to have someone that's walked in my shoes and be a support for my art and my weaving. There are no words to describe it," she said.

"I'm now teaching people how to weave (at the exhibition), so they're now able to be a part of our culture. That's how we are going to keep our culture alive: by sharing it."

Flick Chafer-Smith's painting portrays her totem animal, the pelican, in full flight. Its wings stretch out against winding golden lines, symbolising the fact that "nothing in life is straightforward".

Chafer-Smith's painting of her totem animal, the pelican, in full flight. (ABC News)

"I feel like it's my grandmother, my nanna, flying with me, keeping an eye over me and always being there for the ups and downs," she said.

"And I know that if she was here today, she would be my number one cheerleader."

World.title: $100m plan to use AI to speed up housing
World.content:
Artificial intelligence will be recruited to speed up assessments of housing and energy projects awaiting environmental approval, as the government races to build more homes and ward off a key frustration that is turning voters away from the major parties.

Tuesday's federal budget will include a $105.9 million commitment over four years to develop an AI tool to guide proponents and share environmental data, helping more projects get approved.

A half-billion-dollar package to implement environmental reforms that were passed last year also includes about $250 million to establish the National Environmental Protection Agency.

The commitment is the latest housing measure flagged for the federal budget, which is set to reshape Australia's housing market.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the AI assistance would bring on more supply.

"Our big productivity push is all about getting compliance costs down and cutting red tape, making it easier and faster to build, and making Australia a more attractive place to invest," Mr Chalmers said.

"This is a big investment that will make our economy more productive and will help to get crucial projects going in housing, energy and critical minerals."

Government grasps the nettle on housing

The government had already established a "strike team" to whittle down the backlog of homes awaiting approval, an effort the environment minister says has approved more than 20,000 homes since August last year, and will meet its target of 26,000 approvals by July.

Yesterday, the treasurer announced a $2 billion commitment to support the construction of a further 65,000 homes by funding the roads, water, power, and sewage connections necessary to open new lots.

And tax changes to be confirmed on Tuesday will wind back two major tax breaks for housing investors: the discount on capital gains tax, such as property sales, and the income tax deduction available to housing investors known as "negative gearing".

Labor's massive success at the 2025 federal election has given it the electoral cushion to attempt to break the back of a political issue that has dragged voters away from the major parties over successive elections.

Both the Greens and One Nation have drawn voter support over rising housing and property values that are beyond affordability, particularly among young people and first-home buyers.

Pauline Hanson lashes 'arrogant' critics Pauline Hanson says the major parties "will lose" because of an "arrogant" belief that One Nation is not able to become a mainstream force, following the party's first lower house win this century.

Following the Liberal loss to One Nation in the Farrer by-election, Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg said the major parties were getting what they deserved.

"We are where we deserve to be, over the last 10 years we haven't done enough policy work, and I think the generation of millennials, my generation, are pretty dirty on the major parties and with good reason," Senator Bragg said on Sunday.

"Most of the policies that have been turned out have been junk.

"Our job is to do a better job and actually to do the policy work… it's been about a decade since we've had a decent policy."

Andrew Bragg says the major parties have failed to offer a good housing policy for about a decade. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Labor begins to make case for another broken tax promise

The treasurer, who said in a National Press Club address soon after the 2025 election that he was preparing to "grasp the nettle" and wear some political pain to fix the budget, has flagged that it would include changes to make the housing market and tax system "fairer".

Changes to negative gearing and the capital gains (CGT) discount would be another significant breach of the faith of voters, following a broken promise last term not to amend a package of income tax cuts that would have mostly benefited higher-income earners.

Asked repeatedly on the election campaign trail whether the government would rule out changes to negative gearing or capital gains tax, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese responded with annoyance: "Yes. How hard is it? For the fiftieth time."

Mr Chalmers conceded on Sky News yesterday that Labor's election campaign focused "almost exclusively on supply".

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the federal government has an obligation to explain its reasons for breaking election promises if Tuesday's federal budget does include changes to negative gearing or CGT discounts. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The government has been accused of hiding its intentions during the most recent federal election to hit both tax perks.

Both policies were part of Labor's agenda at the 2019 election, and have become totems of the housing debate inside Labor as much as they have in the electorate.

After Labor's surprise defeat at that election, the policies were set aside.

But since the COVID-19 pandemic, house prices surged, migration swelled as borders reopened, and housing construction slowed in part due to supply chain issues, leading to a tightening in an already tight market — and inflaming the issue.

Mr Chalmers flagged on Sunday that the government was prepared to break its promises to address housing.

"If a government comes to a different view, then the onus is on the government, senior ministers like myself, in explaining why the government has come to a different view," Mr Chalmers said.

"In my case personally, it has become increasingly clear that all of our efforts on housing supply are very important, still the most important thing when it comes to dealing with issues in the housing market, but there are other issues as well."

The treasurer said that since the introduction of the 50 per cent CGT discount two decades ago, house prices had been decoupled from wages.

"Those are facts; I'm not pre-empting announcements on Tuesday night," Mr Chalmers said.

"But the housing market is not working for young people.

"It is locking out too many Australians, and we're not building enough homes … and so I think any responsible government like ours needs to take seriously the very genuine inter-generational concerns that people have and make the housing market fairer and make the tax system fairer as well."

Senator Bragg said it was "insane" to think the housing crisis could be solved with "higher taxes".

"When you've already collapsed housing supply, and you've got higher interest rates, now you have got the prospect of higher taxes in the budget," he said.

"Almost every economist says more tax is going to be bad for housing. Half the cost of a new house goes in government fees, charges and taxes, so why the hell would you consider putting a new tax on something that is already so heavily taxed?"

World.title: ‘I don’t like it’: Trump blast Iran’s ‘unacceptable’ response to US proposal to end war
World.content:
Breaking WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war ‘I don’t like it’: Trump blast Iran’s ‘unacceptable’ response to US proposal to end war Nayera Abdallah , Elwely Elwelly and Idrees Ali Updated May 11, 2026 — 6:28am ,first published 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dubai/Washington: US President Donald Trump has dismissed Iran’s response to the US proposal for peace talks to end the war as “totally unacceptable”. “I have just read the response from Iran’s so-called “Representatives”,” Trump said in a post on TruthSocial abut 6.15 on Monday (Australia time) without giving further detail.. “I don’t like it — TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE!” A poster in Tehran depicts Donald Trump with his mouth gagged by a blue ribbon in the shape of the Strait of Hormuz. Getty Images Earlier, Iranian state media reported that Tehran has sent a response focused on ending the war on all fronts, especially Lebanon, and on the safety of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, without indicating how or when the vital waterway might reopen. Iran also offered to transfer some of its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country, but rejected the idea of dismantling its nuclear facilities, The Wall Street Journal reported.



As part of its proposal, Iran said it would dilute some of its highly enriched uranium and have the rest sent to a third country, the Journal said, citing people familiar with the response – but it also called for guarantees the transferred uranium would be returned if talks fail and ruled out dismantling its facilities. Iran’s response ran several pages, as negotiators proposed an end to the fighting and a gradual reopening of Hormuz, according to the Journal, which noted the two sides remain far apart on the question of Tehran’s nuclear program. Men pray over the bodies of people killed in an Israeli airstrike in the village of Saksakieh, during a funeral procession in the southern port city of Sidon, south Lebanon, on Sunday. AP It followed a US proposal to end fighting before starting talks on more contentious issues, including Iran’s nuclear program. Pakistan, which has been mediating talks over the war, forwarded the Iranian response to the US, a Pakistani official said. There was no immediate US comment.



Despite a month-old ceasefire in the conflict and after some 48 hours of relative calm, hostile drones were detected over several Gulf countries on Sunday, underlining the threat still facing the region. Still, two ships were allowed to pass through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz. Related Article China relations The five ‘Bs’ and three ‘Ts’ at the heart of the Trump-Xi meeting The QatarEnergy-operated carrier Al Kharaitiyat passed safely through and was heading for Pakistan’s Port Qasim, according to data from shipping analytics firm Kpler, the first Qatari vessel carrying liquefied natural gas to cross the strait since the US and Israel started the war on February 28. Sources said earlier the transfer, which offered a modicum of relief to Pakistan after a wave of power blackouts caused by a halt to gas imports, had been approved by Iran to build confidence with Pakistan and with Qatar, another mediator. In addition, a Panama-flagged bulk carrier bound for Brazil that had previously attempted to transit the strait on May 4 passed through, using a route designated by Iran’s armed forces, Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported on Sunday.



With Trump due to visit China this week, there has been mounting pressure to draw a line under the war, which has ignited a global energy crisis and poses a growing threat to the world economy. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war Just weeks ago, Trump said Tehran had ‘agreed to everything’. Why is he now pushing a half-measure? Tehran has largely blocked non-Iranian shipping through the narrow Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried one-fifth of the world’s oil supply and has emerged as one of the central pressure points in the war. Addressing whether combat operations against Iran were over, Trump said in remarks aired on Sunday: “They are defeated, but that doesn’t mean they’re done.” He said Iran had been “playing games” with the US and other countries.



“For 47 years the Iranians have been ‘tapping’ us along, keeping us waiting, killing our people with their roadside bombs, destroying protests, and recently wiping out 42,000 innocent, unarmed protesters, and laughing at our now GREAT AGAIN Country,” he wrote in a social media post. “They will be laughing no longer!” Related Article Middle East at war Trump waits on response to peace plan as Iran accuses US of ‘reckless military adventure’ Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the war was “not over” because there was “more work to be done” to remove enriched uranium from Iran, dismantle enrichment sites and address Iran’s proxies and ballistic missile capabilities. The best way to remove the enriched uranium would be through diplomacy, Netanyahu said in an interview with CBS News’ 60 Minutes, without ruling out removing it by force. “You go in, and you take it out,” he said. “All that is still there, and there’s work to be done.”



Netanyahu declined to elaborate when asked if US or Israeli special forces would enter Iran to remove the nuclear material. He said Trump had indicated that he wished to go into Iran. “I think it can be done physically,” Netanyahu said. “That’s not the problem. That’s a terrifically important mission.” Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a social media post that Iran would “never bow down to the enemy” and would “defend national interests with strength”. Despite diplomatic efforts to break a deadlock, the threat to shipping lanes and the economies of the region remained high. On Sunday, the United Arab Emirates said it intercepted two drones coming from Iran, while Qatar condemned a drone attack that hit a cargo ship coming from Abu Dhabi in its waters. Kuwait said its air defences had dealt with hostile drones that entered its airspace.



Recent days have seen the biggest flare-ups in fighting in and around the strait since a ceasefire began: the UAE came under renewed attack on Friday and sporadic clashes were reported between Iranian forces and US vessels in the strait. Clashes have also continued in southern Lebanon between Israel and Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah, despite a US-brokered ceasefire announced on April 16. Hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah reignited on March 2 when the Lebanese group opened fire after Tehran came under US-Israeli attack. The latest talks between Israel and Lebanon are due to start in Washington on May 14. Though Washington imposed its own blockade on Iranian vessels last month, Tehran has taken its time before responding to calls to end a war that surveys show is unpopular with U.S. voters facing ever-higher gasoline prices. The US has also found little international support, with NATO allies refusing calls to send ships to open the Strait of Hormuz without a full peace deal and an internationally mandated mission.



Britain, which has been working with France on a proposal to ensure safe transit through the strait once the situation stabilises, said on Saturday it was deploying a warship to the Middle East in preparation for such a mission, following a similar move by France. HMS Dragon was dispatched to the Mediterranean in March. Getty Images Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on social media that any stationing of British, French or other warships around the Strait of Hormuz under the pretext of “protecting shipping” would be an escalation and would be met by force. In response, French President Emmanuel Macron said France was standing ready to help the international mission, but “we have never envisaged a military deployment to re-open Hormuz”. World.title: I know my neighbour and the cafe owner in my suburb. It’s all so disgustingly wholesome
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion I know my neighbour and the cafe owner in my suburb. It’s all so disgustingly wholesome Brittney Deguara Social media editor May 11, 2026 — 6:00am

May 11, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The other day, I rushed out the door at 6.15am to catch the bus. I waved goodbye to my daughter and husband, and then smiled and even said “good morning” to the man who was picking up after his dog next to my driveway. Five years ago, a man whose dog had fouled my footpath would have gotten a cold shoulder at best, let alone a smile. But Tarragindi, with its tree-lined streets and pockets of bushland, has turned me into that person. For much of my adult life, I lived in apartments – either here in Brisbane or in New Zealand – and I never knew, or laid eyes on, my neighbours. I liked it that way. But living in this southside hub has changed me. I know, and really like, my neighbour. I say good morning to fellow walkers. I engage with other parents at the playground. And I make small talk with cafe workers. My internal monologue regularly asks of myself, “Who are you?!”



Tucked between Annerley and Moorooka, Tarragindi is a gem of a place. I often joke that everyone either has a dog or a pram – or both. In just a 15-minute walk, you can go through bush to a dog park, into a cafe serving some of the city’s best matcha (we’re looking at you, Lola’s), and to a creek to spot turtles. All this less than 10 kilometres from the CBD. It has such a family-friendly atmosphere that I barely didn’t need to venture out of the area during my 12-month parental leave. In fact, one of the local cafes came to expect me and my sister every Monday with our babies in tow. There’s a ripper scooter park and four playgrounds within walking distance of each other; two primary schools; great doctors at the local clinic; and those cafes are kid-friendly. Tarragindi might not be front of mind when you think of a dinner spot – it’s no Paddington or Bulimba – but it’s holding its own.



Oh Monk dishes up the best beef and cashew stir-fry and coconut rice I’ve ever had, while Georgie’s Corner serves up a mean (and affordable) chicken burger. You can buy a tray of the best cinnamon doughnuts from Davies Bakery, and if you’re feeling bougie, you can browse the aisles of Good Things Grocer for items you won’t find in Woolworths. There’s even a fancy wine bar in a former post office. On the cafe front, the team at Umu Kitchen are the friendliest you’ll ever come across, while Dijon Toasties has come to know my husband by his regular coffee and hash brown order. A koala climbing a tree in Toohey Forest. Ellie McLachlan/Queensland Conservation Council Between meals, you can wander through Toohey Forest to see koalas, goannas and snakes. Or, if you’re afraid of coming across snakes like I am (despite growing up on a farm in north Queensland), you can see photos of them in the local community Facebook group. Formerly known as Sandy Creek, Tarragindi was urbanised in the 1950s during the post-WWII housing boom. At the time, many of the homes were of an Interwar style – asymmetrically designed with a street-facing decorated gable.



We live in a home like this, and while ours has been renovated over the years, it has retained its character. These kinds of houses are slowly disappearing from the streets around us. Instead, mini mansions on 300- to 600-square-metre blocks are taking over. Don’t get me wrong, they’re stunning homes. I walked through one not too long ago and was blown away by the design. But the design is being mimicked by many builders in the area, so it’s all starting to look a little samey. A five-bedder on a 405-square-metre block recently sold for $3.17 million These homes come with huge price tags. A five-bedder on a 405-square-metre block recently sold for $3.17 million. Nearby, one on 614 square metres sold for $4.1 million. It seems every few weeks there’s a post in the community Facebook page with someone selling a house, hoping to find a buyer who will retain its original character. A pipe dream in this flipping economy perhaps?





In fact, I have to pinch myself to think this is where we live. And we’re still only a 20-minute bus ride from the city centre.

World.title: Clubs push back against salary cap concessions for Perth Bears
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Clubs push back against salary cap concessions for Perth Bears Chris Barrett May 11, 2026 — 5:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NRL clubs are set to demand compensation if the Perth Bears are granted salary cap relief to bolster their efforts to build a competitive roster before their 2027 entry into the competition. To this point, the Bears have struggled to attract big-name players. With 2028 competition entrants, the Papua New Guinea Chiefs, able to offer tax-free deals to players, calls for concessions to be granted to Perth continue. Mal Meninga will take charge of the Bears when they join the NRL next season. Trevor Collens It was reported by this masthead that ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys was considering providing assistance to the Bears after lobbying from Perth board members James Bracey and Daniel Dickson and the Rugby League Players’ Association. But any such move would face resistance from existing teams.



“Going back to the initial decision to admit Perth, the clubs raised a number of concerns about the process of getting Perth in and the fact that the NRL would own two clubs in the competition, particularly given we supply them with our most sensitive and commercially confidential information,” South Sydney chief executive Blake Solly said on Sunday. “We needed to have some comfort that those two clubs would be operated at arm’s length. The NRL assured us that both clubs will be salary cap and football department cap compliant. Tyran Wishart is among the signings made by the Perth Bears. Getty Images “That was the basis on which we accepted their entry. If there’s an appetite to move away from that, it needs to involve a discussion with the 17 clubs.” The issue is likely to be a hot topic at Friday’s NRL CEOs conference in Brisbane, which will take place in the hours before Magic Round begins at Suncorp Stadium.



As well as the Bears, the NRL will also own the PNG Chiefs for the first 10 years of their existence as part of a $600 million Australian government-funded package. The decision to add the Bears and the Chiefs to the competition in successive years has presented a major recruitment hurdle for Mal Meninga-led Perth, with PNG able to offer players tax-free wages and third-party deals in the Pacific nation that supercharge their earning power. Jarome Luai (centre) is flanked by PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson and general manager of football Michael Chammas as he signs with the new team. Bringing in two teams within 12 months has also placed pressure on other NRL teams as they try to retain players. Only one new club – the Dolphins, in 2023 – joined the NRL in the previous two decades. Clubs signed off on the PNG deal after being allocated $4 million each in federal taxpayer money.



After expressing reservations about the Perth process, they are likely to push for compensation from the NRL if it backtracks on not providing new teams a salary cap edge. “This was a commitment that Peter and [NRL chief] Andrew [Abdo] made,” Solly said. Toby Sexton will steer the Perth Bears around in their inaugural season. Getty Images “I don’t think any of the clubs are bloody-minded about this. We all want PNG and Perth to succeed. It’s just about recognising the contribution that the 17 existing clubs have made to the growth of the game and our massive investment in pathways and players.” The NRL declined to comment on Sunday.



ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys told this masthead last month the NRL couldn’t carve out exemptions for Perth because “the clubs have always indicated it would be unfair if we did anything other than have the same salary cap for everyone”. Former NSW and Australia halfback Andrew Johns believes the Bears should get a 50 per cent dispensation for two marquee players. Others in the game have discussed whether travel and housing allowances in Perth could be provided. “I think all clubs have always said we’re for the competition being competitive,” Parramatta chief Jim Sarantinos said. “But we agreed, and we were informed that these clubs were coming in based on a set of circumstances, and now those circumstances could change.” Another club CEO, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said on Sunday: “We don’t want them to have any kind of relief because that was the deal. But you could sense something was coming.”



Not all clubs are adamantly against it. Related Article NRL 2026 As PNG Chiefs toast Luai signing, Perth Bears bring in culture expert Canberra chief Don Furner said it would come down to the details. “We’re not saying a blanket no to something that could be a good thing for the game to expand,” he said. “There is no harm in having the discussion and exploring it.” Dolphins CEO Terry Reader said the most difficult part of setting up an NRL franchise was recruitment, “and we had Wayne Bennett [as coach] and were asking players to go to Brisbane”, not the other side of the country.



“We all knew what we signed up to when we came in,” Reader said. “But it’s in the game’s best interest for the new teams to be successful, especially Perth, as it offers another time zone for broadcast revenue. It’s worth having a conversation amongst the clubs and with the NRL.”

World.title: Desperate and in tears, Tabitha had to spend months to find help for a toddler who witnessed murder
World.content:
Exclusive NationalDomestic violence Desperate and in tears, Tabitha had to spend months to find help for a toddler who witnessed murder Amber Schultz May 11, 2026 — 5:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackenzie Anderson’s son was just 23 months old when he witnessed his mother’s murder. Anderson was stabbed 78 times by her ex-partner, Tyler Thompson, in a frenzied attack in the Newcastle suburb of Mayfield in 2022. The toddler had to be bathed of his mother’s blood before he was handed over to his grandmother, Tabitha Acret. Acret said her grandson arrived at her home in “extreme distress”, bashing his head against the wall, screaming and crying from the brutalities he had been witness to. But while dealing with the traumatic loss of her daughter, Acret also had to fight an uphill battle to get her grandson mental health support. Tabitha Acret called more than 20 psychology practices trying to find a clinician who could help her grandson. Danielle Smith She called more than 20 psychology practices, including the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services, but none were willing to take the family on as clients.



“For six months, I was running around trying to find a psychologist, and I was just told no, your case is too complex.” Eventually, “desperate and in tears”, she called an occupational therapist who agreed to take the child on, and his behaviour has started to improve. “Children don’t witness violence, they experience it, and they’re also primary victims,” Acret said. “They need to be recognised as victims by the law, and the emotional damage needs to be recognised.” Acret, who has been paying $300 out of pocket for years for the sessions, also struggled to find help for herself in the crime’s aftermath.



Mackenzie Anderson was murdered by her ex-partner in 2022. Instagram She’s also calling for a family or victim navigator to be assigned to the family to help them navigate the complexities of the health, social and court systems, and assist with the bureaucracy involved following a crime. “It would have been nice if somebody could have come to my house and explained what the steps are, and then helped me get a counsellor, instead of me having to do it,” she said. Act for Kids executive director Tom McIntyre said children who experienced domestic and family violence were more likely to have emotional and behavioural problems in childhood, adolescence and adulthood than children who had not experienced it. “[It] can lead to long-term trauma in children, which can show up in schools, the healthcare system and in the relationships young people make in the community,” McIntyre said.



“We need to ensure the voices of young people are heard and recognised, and to bring about healing, we need to address the effects on children and young people who experience domestic and family violence.” Related Article Exclusive

Domestic violence Molly asked for help before her murder. This group thinks it knows what needs to be done The 2022 Australian Personal Safety Survey found that one in eight adults had witnessed violence between their parents or caregivers before the age of 15. Young people who witness parental domestic violence are more likely to become victims of domestic violence as adults. University of Melbourne Associate Professor of Social Work Kristin Diemer said supports have traditionally focused on a mother experiencing family and domestic violence. “We feel that if we protect the mother, she will protect the child, which is asking an awful lot of a mother going through trauma to also support children going through trauma,” she said.



“We have a history of not creating appropriate services for children themselves, and we don’t have the service support easily accessible for young people and children.” Diemer said that being able to talk to people who are independent of their family helps children process and recover. “Children and young people will understand stress and strain in a relationship regardless of whether they actively view it,” she said. “It penetrates into how they live their lives.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: ‘A complete disconnect’: Council set to back down on inner-city bike plan
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLocal council ‘A complete disconnect’: Council set to back down on inner-city bike plan Rachael Dexter May 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A controversial plan to block most car and truck traffic on a large stretch of a main road in Melbourne’s inner north looks set to be shelved after public backlash, sparking accusations of weakness from cycling advocates and cautious optimism from residents opposed to the so-called bicycle street. The proposal to transform a 1.1-kilometre stretch of Wellington Street by blocking access to most cars is now recommended to be shelved. Yarra City Council is to vote on it on Tuesday night. The stretch currently has painted bike lanes and two-way vehicle traffic. Since last year, the council has been consulting on two options to redesign the section of Wellington Street between Johnston Street in Collingwood and Queens Parade in Clifton Hill to prioritise cycling and pedestrians. The so-called bicycle street would either be a shared zone with a 30km/h speed limit where motorists share the main traffic lanes with cyclists, or dedicated bike lanes featuring physical “protected” barriers in Clifton Hill and painted lanes in Collingwood.



Both options include physical barriers such as garden beds and concrete kerbs to block vehicles from driving the full length of the stretch, and would require residents of Wellington Street to use side-street diversions to reach their homes. They would also reduce on-street parking and change the number of trees on the 1.1-kilometre stretch across both suburbs. But there has been major community division over the plan. In a survey conducted by the council that received 1654 unique responses, 62 per cent (including non-locals who travel through the area) backed some form of traffic blocking. That number dropped among locals, however, with 50 per cent of Collingwood respondents and 47 per cent of Clifton Hill locals not supporting either option. Cumulative petitions containing more than 2560 signatures against the plans have also been submitted to the council, against a 780-signature open letter supporting the project. Alexandra Lamb speaks to supporters of the proposal at a meeting in March. Luis Enrique Ascui Council planners are now suggesting councillors back a substantially watered-down package that includes minor safety works, repainting the bike lanes, upgrading a school crossing and investigating a 30km/h speed limit.



Alexandra Lamb, organiser of the Say Yes to a New Wellington St campaign which is in favour of traffic diversions, said her group was appalled by the recommendation. “Yarra City Council officers should be embarrassed by their backflip, which looks like weakness at best ...,” she said. “There is a complete disconnect between the analysis of the report, the research and community consultation that went into it, and its recommendations.” The council officers’ new report presents different statistics, which has allowed both sides to claim the evidence supports their case.



Officers argue that traffic diversions to side streets are unlikely, asserting that drivers will stick to arterial routes like Hoddle Street, or that trips will evaporate. However, the report simultaneously concedes that preliminary modelling predicts a potential 56 per cent surge in daily traffic on Gold Street – roughly 900 vehicles extra a day on the residential street. The report also concedes the watered-down changes would be “less impactful” in addressing “the core issue of high traffic volumes and the safety issues”. Sebastian Guiney, leader of the Oppose Wellington St Closure campaign, welcomed the “significant shift” from the council, but said his group would not celebrate until the final vote.



“The statement that the tactical works ‘do not prohibit a street transformation option being progressed in the future’ is concerning,” Guiney said. “We believe that given the level of community opposition ... this issue should be put to bed.” The opposition group cited concern for the viability of two service stations on the strip if traffic were cut, as well as traffic increases on Gold Street, which is home to a park, a daycare facility and aged care facility, and is one of the main drop-off spots for Clifton Hill Primary School. “Going forward, we would also like to see council officers take a more balanced approach to these proposals and genuinely consult widely with the community, rather than trying to pull the wool over the community’s eyes and push through projects that are unpopular with local residents and businesses,” Guiney said. Opponents of the Wellington Street closure gather for a rally at Little Sam’s Service Station in March. Simon Schluter



The plans were to be the final stages of the council’s gradual upgrade of Wellington Street. It has already completed two stages south of Johnston Street. However, those sections between Victoria Parade and Johnston Street do not include the traffic blocking that was proposed for the latter stages. Tuesday night’s meeting is expected to be inundated with proponents and opponents attempting to persuade councillors before the vote. Related Article City life The 9km corridor that’s recorded 279 cyclist crashes but still doesn’t have a protected bike lane Mayor Stephen Jolly has previously said the level of interest in the issue was unprecedented, telling a council meeting this year that he had “never seen Collingwood so passionate about something one way or another”.
